g1-bijvoeglijk-naamwoord-aanwijzend.name: The adjective after a demonstrative + material adjectives (-en)

g1-inversie.name: Inversion — verb before subject when something else is in first position

g1-meervoud-uitzonderingen.name: Irregular plural nouns — -eren, sound shift, Latin plurals, nouns without a plural

A.name: -eren
A.how: Some het-words form their plural with -eren instead of -en.

B.name: Sound shift
B.how: The short vowel becomes long in the plural, because it ends up in an open syllable (da-gen).

C.name: Latin plurals
C.how: Latin nouns keep a Latin plural: -cus becomes -ci, and -um becomes -a.

D.name: No plural
D.how: Some nouns have no plural, such as uncountable substances. They take a singular verb, and 'veel' goes with the singular.

g1-werkwoordsvorm-per-plek.name: Which verb FORM belongs in which slot (conjugated / stem / infinitive)

A.name: modal verb + infinitive at the end
A.how: willen, kunnen, mogen, moeten (and zullen) are irregular: ik/jij/hij wil · kan · mag · moet, wij/jullie/zij willen · kunnen · mogen · moeten. The modal is the finite verb; the infinitive goes to the END of the sentence, and niet goes right before that infinitive. Question with jij: kan/kun jij? — with u: kunt u? / wilt u?

g1-bijvoeglijk-naamwoord.name: The adjective: when it takes -e, and how the spelling changes

A.name: adjective + -e
A.how: An adjective in front of a noun gets -e: with every de-word, with het-words after de/het/dit/dat/mijn…, and in the plural.

B.name: indefinite het-word: no -e
B.how: A singular het-word that is indefinite keeps the adjective bare — after een, and also after geen, welk, elk, ieder.

C.name: not before a noun: no -e
C.how: After zijn/worden/vinden, or describing how someone does something, the adjective never gets -e.

D.name: spelling when -e is added
D.how: Adding -e opens the syllable, so the spelling adjusts: short vowel doubles the consonant, a double long vowel loses a letter, f→v, s→z; -ig and diphthongs don't change.

E.name: fixed combinations: no -e
E.how: Some adjective + het-word pairs are fixed terms and never take -e, even after het. Bart's advice on the slide: no need to learn them — just recognise them.

F.name: uncountable het-word: no -e
F.how: An uncountable het-word (water, bier, geld) with no article — or after veel, meer, weinig, minder — is indefinite, so no -e. Uncountable de-words still get -e.

g2-te-iets-die-bijvoeglijk.name: te, iets and die with an adjective (without a noun)

A.name: te + adjective = too
A.how: te right before an adjective or adverb means 'too'. Don't confuse it with te before an infinitive (te lezen, om … te vertellen), which just marks the verb.

B.name: iets / wat / niets … + adjective + s
B.how: After a quantity word — iets, wat, niets, veel, weinig, genoeg, allerlei, meer, minder, voldoende — an adjective with no noun after it gets -s. English says 'something nice'; Dutch says iets leuks.

C.name: die + adjective-e, noun left out
C.how: When the noun is already clear, Dutch can drop it and keep the adjective with its -e: Welke appel? Die grote. Bart's advice on the slide: when you speak, just add the noun.

g2-verleden-tijd-of-perfectum.name: Past tense or present perfect? (imperfectum vs perfectum)

B.name: past tense or present perfect?
B.how: Don't pick the tense the way English would — Bart's slide says it in bold. Present perfect (heeft gezegd) = a single event, the result, a plain fact, fine without a time. Past tense (zei, kreeg, kon) = a story or sequence (en toen? daarna …), a habit, a process, and only with a time indication (gisteren, vanavond).
